title: The loop holds the Mac awake the whole time it is working
goal: You answered a card on 2026-09-20 asking whether the loop should stop your Mac locking itself while it works, and you chose to keep it awake. Nothing was built, and the Mac locked itself half an hour after you answered. It has been locked ever since, which costs 163 of 544 scripted walks every sweep and puts a caveat on every picture in every audit you are asked to read. Make the loop hold the machine awake for as long as it is working, not only for the forty minutes a sweep is running.
notes:
VERIFIED on 2026-09-21 during the digest pass.

The answer: decision trim... no, decision id a-hundred-and-fifteen-walks-fail-on-code-that-pa-while-the-loop-is-working-throug, question "While the loop is working through the night, should it stop your Mac locking itself?", resolved 2026-09-20T17:32:21Z, choice awake-while-working ("Keep it awake while the loop works").

What is actually built: grep caffeinate across Scripts/ and queue/bin/ finds it in exactly one place, Scripts/playtest-all.sh:121, `caffeinate -d -i -t $(awake_seconds) &`, started by hold_awake() for the length of one sweep and released by its EXIT trap. queue/bin/go-loop.sh (551 lines) has no caffeinate in it at all. So the machine is held awake for the roughly 75 minutes a sweep runs and let go in every gap between them.

SPLIT OUT of a-hundred-and-fifteen-walks-fail-on-code-that-pa on purpose. That task is the large one (make a walk answer the same way locked or not, by taking accessibility out of the walk harness step kind by step kind) and it has been open since 2026-09-15. This is the small concrete thing the user actually asked for, and burying it in the large one is why it has not happened.

It does NOT unlock the Mac and must not try. A Mac already locked stays locked until somebody logs in; this only stops the NEXT lock.
acceptance: The go loop holds the Mac awake from the moment it starts working until it stops, covering the gaps between sweeps as well as the sweeps themselves
It never fights the sweep's own hold: one of them holds at a time and neither kills the other's, and neither kills a hold the user started by hand
Stopping the loop, or killing it, releases the hold; a check after a stop shows nothing left holding the machine awake
A run started while the screen is already locked says so plainly on the Grants line and does not pretend the hold fixed it, because nothing but a person can unlock a Mac
Proved by leaving the loop running across at least two idle gaps and reading CGSSessionScreenIsLocked before and after

log.note: owns no walks; the ones it names are examples

Adversarial pass BEFORE building. The obvious build is 'caffeinate -d -i -t <long> in the loop', which is what the sweep does. Three ways it goes wrong on somebody else's machine: (1) a -t long enough for an overnight loop is a hold that outlives a killed loop by hours, and the loop is killed (ctrl-c, a reload, a crash) far more often than a sweep is; (2) two holds is two things to put down and one of them to get wrong, and the sweep already takes one; (3) a pattern kill (pkill caffeinate) takes the user's own hold with it. So: caffeinate -d -i -w $$, which is released by the loop's pid going away and therefore needs no trap to be correct; the sweep defers to it rather than stacking; and every put-down is by recorded pid with a pid-reuse guard. Rejected -u outright: it posts user activity and would light up a display the user had already put to sleep, at whatever hour the loop reached it.

Built. queue/bin/go-loop.sh takes one hold at startup (hold_awake) and releases it in cleanup and on EXIT; RELOADING=1 keeps it across the exec so a reload adopts the same caffeinate from queue/.loop-awake.pid instead of stacking. Scripts/playtest-all.sh defers when PHOTONZ_LOOP_AWAKE_PIDFILE names a live hold and writes no pidfile of its own, which is exactly what tells sweep.sh stop_the_run and sweep-recover.mjs there is nothing of theirs to release. Scripts/probe-app.sh puts it on the Grants line and, under a lock, says in three lines that the hold stops the NEXT lock and cannot undo this one. queue/.loop-awake.pid gitignored.

VERIFIED. queue/bin/awake-drill.sh: 22 checks, all green. Live, all on this machine: (1) a real loop across three idle gaps held the same caffeinate pid continuously for 175s and released on a clean stop with the pidfile gone (BEFORE screen=locked caffeinates=[] / t=8s..175s heldpid=61584 assertion=2 / AFTER caffeinates=[] pidfile=gone); (2) a real loop SIGKILLed released its hold in under a second (caffeinate 66502 alive=no, all caffeinates=[]); (3) a real loop reloaded onto an edited copy kept ONE hold with the same pid (before hold=79843, after reload hold=79843, reloads=1) and released it on kill -9; (4) a real loop stopped with TERM released it and removed the pidfile (took 46s, because the loop is inside its idle sleep when the signal lands, which is how it already behaved). Grants line with the hold on: '==> Grants: probe Screen Recording granted - this terminal Accessibility denied - screen locked - the loop is holding this Mac awake', followed by three lines saying the hold does NOT undo this lock. redline-walk exit 0 with 14 real window captures, so the Grants change did not disturb the launch path. Scripts/test.sh: 8639 tests in 686 suites passed.

left rough: if the loop is SIGKILLed WHILE a sweep is running, the sweep is orphaned (it always was) and is now also unheld, because it deferred to a hold that has just gone. Bounded by queue/bin/sweep-recover.mjs, which puts orphaned sweeps down at the top of every sweep.sh verb, and by ctrl-c being the normal stop (it signals the group, so sweep.sh winds itself down properly). Not filed: it is one more symptom of an already-broken state that has a named recovery, and the alternative is two holds, which is the thing this task was asked to avoid.
left rough: the dashboard says nothing about the hold. Only the loop's own window and the probe's Grants line do. Not filed: nobody is stopped by it and the audit asks the user whether they want it.
